It is of the fifth order, illuminating the entire horizon. The fog signal is a bell, which is struck by machinery one blow every ten seconds. During May a small oil house, a platform for coal, etc., under the wharf, and steps leading to the ground, were built.
Roe Island, Suisun Bay.establishes: Roe Island station put in operation 16 February 1891; fixed white fifth-order light shown from a lantern on the dwelling roof; fog bell struck by machinery one blow every ten seconds. Contractors named: M. A. Graham (ironwork), California Bridge Company (buildings and wharf). Board station number 814.

Roe Island.quote: 852. Roe Island, Suisun Bay, California.—A windmill and pump were placed on the outer end of the wharf and connection was made by pipe with the cistern to bring in a supply of fresh water. The lantern parapet was incased in redwood to prevent leakage. This island being subject to overflow at times of high water, a levee 3½ feet high by 8 feet at the base was built around the reservation. This levee was cracked in April by a severe earthquake, and it was repaired by the keeper.
Roe Island.establishes: A levee was built around the Roe Island reservation in FY1892 and was cracked by a severe earthquake in April 1892 — a dated seismic observation from a Suisun Bay station, repaired by the keeper.

Table Bluff / Humboldt (re-establishment.station: Table Bluff / Humboldt (re-establishment) — authorization and site
Table Bluff / Humboldt (re-establishment.quote: 821. Humboldt, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—Congress at its last session appropriated $25,000 for the reestablishment of this station on a new site. The Light-House Board having decided that the best interests of navigation would be subserved by locating the new station on Table Bluff, a point about 4 miles south of the present light, the inspector and engineer of this district visited the place on May 8, 1891, and selected a site for the station. The owner of the selected land refused to sell for less than $5,000 for about 10 acres of land and the right of way for a road from the county road to the proposed station. This price was deemed exorbitant, and measures were initiated to acquire title by condemnation.
Table Bluff / Humboldt (re-establishment.establishes: Congress appropriated $25,000 for moving the Humboldt light station; the Board chose Table Bluff, about 4 miles south of the old light; site selected on the ground 8 May 1891; the landowner's $5,000 asking price for ~10 acres was refused and condemnation begun. This is the Board's own statement of WHY Table Bluff was chosen: 'the best interests of navigation'.

Table Bluff / Humboldt.quote: 859. Humboldt, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—The suit brought to obtain, by condemnation, title to the land needed for the reestablishment of this station on Table Bluff was withdrawn and a compromise was made with the owner whereby the United States secured for $2,220 some 10 acres of land, together with the right to take water from an adjacent spring.
Table Bluff / Humboldt.establishes: The condemnation suit was dropped and the Table Bluff site (about 10 acres plus spring water rights) was bought for $2,220. Bids for construction were opened 21 March 1892. OCR-derived; the dollar figure in particular should be re-checked against the leaf image before publication.

Table Bluff / Humboldt.station: Table Bluff / Humboldt — completion and first lighting
Table Bluff / Humboldt.quote: 885. Humboldt, near the western edge of Table Bluff, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—The reestablishment of this station on the new site at Table Bluff, commenced last year, was continued until October 5, 1892, when it was satisfactorily completed. The lens and one fog-signal boiler were kept at the old station until October 31, the date set for starting the new station. On October 31, the light was exhibited from the new station and the old station was abandoned. The new station on Table Bluff consists of a keeper's dwelling and tower combined, a double dwelling for the assistant keepers, a fog-signal building containing two boilers and engines and a coal shed.
Table Bluff / Humboldt.establishes: Table Bluff light station structurally complete 5 October 1892; light first exhibited from the new station and the old Humboldt station abandoned on 31 October 1892. Lens and one fog-signal boiler were transferred from the old station. Plant described: combined dwelling-and-tower, double assistant keepers' dwelling, fog-signal building with two boilers and engines, coal shed, ~10-acre fenced reservation.

St. George Reef (Northwest Seal Rock).station: St. George Reef (Northwest Seal Rock) — 1891 season, funding stoppage, $81,000 deficiency appropriation
St. George Reef (Northwest Seal Rock).quote: 824. St. George Reef, Northwest Seal Rock, seacoast of California.—By the middle of the first month of the fiscal year all the stone required for the completion of this work was quarried and cut, when the available funds not being sufficient to warrant resumption of construction, all work was shut down, the plant stored at the stone yard, and that place left in charge of a watchman. During the year the specifications and drawings for the metalwork for the tower were prepared and contract was made with the Phoenix Iron Company of Trenton, N. J., for its construction. By the end of the fiscal year it was completed and on its way to San Francisco. An item in the general deficiency act approved September 30, 1890, appropriated $81,000 for the completion of this station.
St. George Reef (Northwest Seal Rock).establishes: Work at St. George Reef was shut down in July 1890 for want of money; the tower metalwork was contracted to the Phoenix Iron Company of Trenton, N.J.; a general deficiency act of 30 September 1890 appropriated $81,000 to finish the station; the steamer Sunol was chartered in April 1891 and construction resumed 1 May 1891. Board station number 824.

St. George Reef.station: St. George Reef — the Board's summary of the whole 1883–1891 construction
St. George Reef.quote: 862. St. George Reef, Northwest Seal Rock, seacoast of California.—There will be found in an appendix to this volume an interesting description by Mr. A. Ballantyne, superintendent of construction of the Northwest Seal Rock Light-Station, California, of the early history, annual progress, and many incidents and facts connected with this work. There have been prepared from the office records, also, tabulated statements showing in detail the cost of its different parts. The work was commenced in 1883 and it was completed in 1891. The long time required for its construction and completion, together with the incidental expenses, were due, in a great measure, to inadequate appropriations.
St. George Reef.establishes: The Board's own summary verdict on St. George Reef: begun 1883, completed 1891, and the nine-year duration and inflated incidental cost were 'due, in a great measure, to inadequate appropriations.' Also: stone was quarried from granite boulders on Mad River near Humboldt Bay, nearly 100 miles from the site; dressed at a stoneyard at the entrance to Humboldt Bay; 1,339 dressed dimension stones in the face of the structure; three-sixteenths-inch joints; credit given to David Chalmers (foreman of stonecutters), Thomas W. Brown (quarrying), and A. Ballantyne (superintendent of construction); work directed by Capt. A. H. Payson, Corps of Engineers, until late 1887.

St. George Reef.station: St. George Reef — total appropriated (Appendix No. 5, report of A. Ballantyne, Superintendent of Construction, printed in the Board's annual report)
St. George Reef.quote: No attempt was made to work at the rock during the season of 1890, as the available funds would not warrant it, and no further appropriation was made until September 30, 1890, when $81,000 became available. This made a total of $721,000 appropriated, which was the estimated cost of the structure.
St. George Reef.establishes: Total appropriated for St. George Reef light station = $721,000, stated as equal to the estimated cost of the structure. Appropriation sequence given in the same appendix: $30,000 by the act of 7 July 1884; $40,000 by the act of 3 March [1885]; no appropriation in 1886; $120,000 available 4 March 1887; a further appropriation available April 1888; $200,000 approved 2 March 1889; $81,000 available 30 September 1890. Season-by-season costs also given, e.g. '$46,009.17' expended during the summer of 1883. NOTE: this is the superintendent's report printed as an appendix to the Board's report, not the Board's own narrative — cite it as such. Three detailed cost tables follow on pp. 276–280, but their columns are badly scrambled in the OCR and should be read from the page images, not the text file.

St. George Reef.station: St. George Reef — fog signal established
St. George Reef.quote: 862. St. George Reef, California.—The 12-inch steam whistles, in duplicate, have been operated some 139 hours since the time of their establishment, December 1, 1891, consuming about 13 tons of coal.
St. George Reef.establishes: The St. George Reef fog signal — 12-inch steam whistles in duplicate — was established 1 December 1891, ten and a half months before the light itself was first exhibited. Operated 139 hours in its first partial season on about 13 tons of coal.

St. George Reef.quote: 888. St. George Reef, Pacific Ocean, on Northwest Seal Rock, St. George Reef, California.—This station was completed last year, except the lens, which had not then been received. During July the lens reached San Francisco, and in August it was taken by the light-house tender to the station, where it was erected. The light is of the first order, flashing alternately red and white, with fifteen seconds interval between flashes, illuminating the entire horizon. It was exhibited for the first time on October 20, 1892.
St. George Reef.establishes: St. George Reef light first exhibited 20 October 1892; first order, flashing alternately red and white at fifteen-second intervals, illuminating the entire horizon. Lens arrived San Francisco July 1892, carried to the rock by the light-house tender in August 1892. A footnote on the same page adds: 'On July 22, 1893, an easy landing was made on the rock. The entire station was found to be in excellent condition. It is now amply provided with coal and supplies.'

St. George Reef fog signal.station: St. George Reef fog signal — first full-year running time
St. George Reef fog signal.quote: 888. St. George Reef, California.—The 12-inch steam whistle, in duplicate, was in operation some 405 hours, and consumed about 27 tons of coal.
St. George Reef fog signal.establishes: First full fiscal year of fog-signal operation at St. George Reef: 405 hours, ~27 tons of coal. OCR-derived, not image-verified.

Punta Gorda (proposed light and fog sign.station: Punta Gorda (proposed light and fog signal) — the Board's standing recommendation
Punta Gorda (proposed light and fog sign.quote: —. Punta Gorda, between Shelter Cove and Cape Mendocino, seacoast of California.—The following recommendation, which was made in the Board's last two annual reports, is renewed: Between Shelter Cove and Punta Gorda there are several dangerous sunken rocks off the shore that add to the hazards of navigation. In ordinary dark nights the overhanging mountains keep the shore line in dark shadow and confuse the best navigator as to his distance from shore, so that it is impossible to make out this high rounding point, either from the south or from the north. Moreover, from reports made to the Coast and Geodetic Survey, it appears that little is known as to the currents of this part of the coast. The conclusion is reached, therefore, that the interests of commerce and navigation require that a light and fog signal be established at or near Punta Gorda, Cal. It is estimated that the work will cost $40,000.
Punta Gorda (proposed light and fog sign.establishes: The Board's full stated reason for wanting a Punta Gorda station, and its $40,000 estimate. The phrase 'made in the Board's last two annual reports' dates the first Punta Gorda recommendation to the FY1889 report. The identical text is renewed in 1892 ('last three annual reports', p. 187), 1893 ('last four', p. 166), and 1894 ('last five', p. 186).

Punta Gorda.station: Punta Gorda — the casualty the Board cited
Punta Gorda.quote: The British steamer Bawnmore struck on a rock at Punta Gorda during a fog and sunk. She is now being pumped out and will be saved. This could not have happened had there been a fog signal at this point.
Punta Gorda.establishes: The Board appended a specific wreck to its Punta Gorda argument: the British steamer Bawnmore struck a rock at Punta Gorda in fog and sank during FY1893, and the Board asserted flatly that a fog signal there would have prevented it.

Punta Gorda.quote: Punta Gorda light and fog-signal station, California 40, 000. 00
Punta Gorda.establishes: Punta Gorda carried in the Board's formal estimates to Congress at $40,000 for FY1893. OCR-derived from a figures table; verify against the image before quoting the cents.

Punta Gorda.report_year: FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; 'Report of the Operations of the Light-House Board', Twelfth District, uncompleted works)
Punta Gorda.quote: Punta Gorda, Cal.—The act approved May 27, 1908, appropriated $60,000 for a light and fog-signal station at or near Four-Mile Creek, near Punta Gorda. During the latter part of June, 1910, the contractor commenced work on the construction of the buildings, which embrace a light tower, a fog-signal building, and three keepers' dwellings and barn. At the close of the fiscal year 1910 the sum of $5,832.47 had been expended and obligated under the appropriation for preliminary examination, survey, purchase of site, purchase of lens and accessories, and incidental expenses. Of the amount stated, $2,810.10 had been expended. The contractor has made excavations and placed the forms for the foundations for the fog-signal building and carpenter and blacksmith shop. The excavation for two dwellings was completed. January 1, 1911, is the date on which the light will probably be ready for operation.
Punta Gorda.establishes: Appropriation of $60,000 by act of 27 May 1908; site 'at or near Four-Mile Creek, near Punta Gorda'; construction begun late June 1910; the Board's forecast first-lighting date of 1 January 1911. This is NOT an establishment statement — the actual lighting fell in FY1912, whose report I could not obtain.

Punta Gorda.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Punta Gorda.quote: Punta Gorda, just south of Four-Mile Creek near Punta Gorda, seacoast of California.—The recommendation made in the Board's last five annual reports that an appropriation of $60,000 be made to establish a light and fog-signal at or near Punta Gorda, California, is renewed.
Punta Gorda.establishes: That by FY1907 the Board had been asking for a Punta Gorda station in each of its last five annual reports (i.e. since roughly FY1902) at an estimated $60,000 — the figure Congress finally voted on 27 May 1908.

Quarry Point, Angel Island (PROPOSED fog.station: Quarry Point, Angel Island (PROPOSED fog signal — never built in this era) — first recommendation
Quarry Point, Angel Island (PROPOSED fog.quote: Mariners have asked that Quarry Point be selected for the fog-signal station, because, to make a start up river in a fog, it is necessary to make Angel Island to get a departure. After careful examination the Board reached the conclusion that a fog signal at this locality would be a decided aid to mariners. In view of the great economy of establishing and maintaining a large fog bell here instead of a steam fog signal, it decided in favor of the former. It is estimated that it will cost $6,000 to establish this fog bell, and it is recommended that an appropriation of this amount be made therefor.
Quarry Point, Angel Island (PROPOSED fog.establishes: IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: 'Quarry Point, Angel Island' is a SEPARATE, never-built proposal, first advanced in the FY1892 report and renewed verbatim every year through FY1901 — it is not the Point Knox station. The passage states the Board's reasoning (Angel Island is the departure mark for the up-river run in fog; the Southampton Shoal passage is narrow; casualties cited include the ferry steamer Contra Costa, the ships E. B. Sutton, Eleanor Margaret and Maulsden) and its $6,000 fog-bell estimate. That this is the FIRST statement is established two ways: the 1892 text carries no 'is renewed' formula, and the renewal counter runs 1893 'last annual report' (1), 1894 'last two', 1895 'last three', 1896 'last four', 1897 'last five', 1899 'last seven', 1900 'last eight', 1901 'last nine' — arithmetic that resolves exactly to a 1892 origin.

Quarry Point, Angel Island.station: Quarry Point, Angel Island — the Board changes its mind about bells
Quarry Point, Angel Island.quote: Much complaint has been made by mariners that the bell fog-signals used at the light and fog-signal stations in this vicinity are not sufficiently far-reaching. The Board is now of opinion that the signal to be used at Quarry Point should be of a more efficient character than a bell, particularly as all the commerce bound to Vallejo, Mare Island, and the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers must pass close to a bold and rocky promontory. It is believed that it should be a first-class compressed-air siren, similar in power to the fog-signal recently established at Point Arguello. Quarry Point being part of the military reservation at Fort McDowell on Angel Island, no expense for its site would be incurred. It is estimated that such a signal, with quarters for the keepers, could be built for $12,000, and the board recommends that an appropriation of that amount be made therefor.
Quarry Point, Angel Island.establishes: This is the single most useful Board statement on California fog signals in this era: after nine years of recommending a cheap large bell, the Board reverses itself in 1901 because 'much complaint has been made by mariners that the bell fog-signals used at the light and fog-signal stations in this vicinity are not sufficiently far-reaching,' and asks instead for a first-class compressed-air siren at $12,000. It also confirms Quarry Point lay inside the Fort McDowell military reservation, so no site purchase was needed.

Angel Island fog-signal station (the Poi.station: Angel Island fog-signal station (the Point Knox station) — existence and character
Angel Island fog-signal station (the Poi.quote: 1008. Angel Island fog-signal station, San Francisco Bay, California.—A fence was built around the dwelling, and the yard in front was covered with concrete. A small frame storehouse was built at the base of the hill to replace one carried away by a landslide. Various repairs were made.
Angel Island fog-signal station (the Poi.establishes: The station the brief calls 'Point Knox' is carried by the Board simply as 'Angel Island fog-signal station' (Board number 1008 in 1897; 886 in 1893; 902 in 1895; 24 in 1899). In 1897 it was still a FOG-SIGNAL station only, with no light — which is why no 'date of first lighting' exists for it before 1900. Landslides on the hillside were a recurring problem. NOTE: the Board's establishment statement for this station belongs to the FY1886 report, which I could not obtain.

Angel Island.station: Angel Island — a light finally added
Angel Island.quote: Angel Island light-station, San Francisco Bay, California.—A lens-lantern light November 26, 1900.
Angel Island.establishes: A lens-lantern light was first shown at the Angel Island (Point Knox) station on 26 November 1900 — i.e. the fog-signal station of the 1880s became a light station only at the very end of this era. Point Montara and Lime Point received lens-lantern lights on the same date. Corroborated in the same volume at p. 197: '28. Angel Island, San Francisco Bay, California.—A fixed red lens-lantern light was established.' The 1900 report (p. 179) had foreshadowed it: '26. Angel Island, San Francisco Bay, California.—A fixed red lens-lantern light will be installed as soon as the lantern is received.' (that 1900 sentence is OCR-only).

San Francisco Harbor light-vessel.station: San Francisco Harbor light-vessel — authorization and cost
San Francisco Harbor light-vessel.quote: —. San Francisco Harbor light-vessel, off San Francisco Bar, California.—By the act approved June 11, 1896, $40,000 was appropriated, and a contract was authorized not to exceed $80,000, for constructing, equipping, and outfitting complete for service a first-class steam light-vessel with steam fog-signal for this station. The proper measures are being taken for its construction. It is estimated that $40,000, in addition to the amount already appropriated, will be needed to finish this vessel. Recommendation is made that this amount be appropriated therefor.
San Francisco Harbor light-vessel.establishes: The San Francisco lightship station was authorized by the act of 11 June 1896: $40,000 appropriated with contract authority to $80,000, for a first-class steam light-vessel with steam fog signal. A further $40,000 was needed and asked for. The same report, p. 26, notes the parallel authorization for a light-vessel off Fire Island, New York.

San Francisco Harbor light-vessel No. 70.station: San Francisco Harbor light-vessel No. 70 — construction
San Francisco Harbor light-vessel No. 70.quote: 1004. San Francisco Harbor light-vessel No. 70, off San Francisco Bar, California.—This vessel is being built at Portland, Oregon. An appropriation of $40,000 was made by the act approved June 4, 1897, for her completion. Contract was made after due advertisement on January 23, 1897, with the lowest bidder to deliver the vessel in November, 1897.
San Francisco Harbor light-vessel No. 70.establishes: Lightship No. 70 was built at Portland, Oregon; the completing $40,000 came by the act of 4 June 1897; contract let 23 January 1897 for November 1897 delivery. Total federal outlay therefore $80,000. Detailed specification follows in the same entry: steel-framed, wood-planked hull, 112 ft x 18.5 ft x 22 ft 1.5 in, 350 ihp single-cylinder engine, four-bladed screw, electric masthead flashing lights, Crosby steam chime whistle, ~350 gross tons. OCR-derived; not image-verified.

San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.station: San Francisco light-vessel No. 70 — placed on station
San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.quote: 20. San Francisco light-vessel No. 70, California.—This composite steam light-vessel, built in 1897–98, of about 400 tons burden, was placed on her station April 7, 1898, in 18¼ fathoms of water, about 3½ miles outside the bar off the entrance to San Francisco Harbor. She carries a steam fog-signal and shows electric lights.
San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.establishes: The San Francisco lightship station was established 7 April 1898, when Light-Vessel No. 70 took up a mooring in 18¼ fathoms about 3½ miles outside the bar. Steam fog signal and electric lights. Same volume p. 183: 'San Francisco light vessel, No. 70, California.—The 12-inch steam chime whistle was in operation some 1,045 hours, and consumed about 83 tons of coal.'

San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.station: San Francisco light-vessel No. 70 — first withdrawal for repairs
San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.quote: San Francisco light-vessel, entrance to San Francisco Harbor, California.—Light-vessel No. 70 withdrawn for repairs and station marked by a first-class can buoy September 20; light-house tender Madrono moored on station, characteristics of lights and fog signal changed September 28; light-vessel No. 70 replaced on station, characteristics of lights and fog signal restored, and Madrono withdrawn October 8, 1899.
San Francisco light-vessel No. 70.establishes: First interruption of the new San Francisco lightship station: No. 70 off station 20 September – 8 October 1899, eighteen days, with the tender Madrono serving as relief light-vessel from 28 September. Oil lamps were substituted for the electric lights 5–11 May 1900 and the fog whistle was silent 18–26 June 1900. OCR-derived; not image-verified.

Oakland Harbor.quote: 872, 873. Oakland Harbor, entrance to Oakland Harbor, California.—The Board decided to dispense with the inner red light, situated just outside the north training wall, about three fourths of a mile to the eastward of the outer white light, and to establish instead a red light on the southern side of the entrance, in the prolongation of the south jetty, about 240 feet outside its outer end. The beacon consists of 4 piles standing in 13 feet of water at low tide, surmounted by a square structure about 7 feet wide by 7 feet high.
Oakland Harbor.establishes: In FY1893 the Board reorganized the Oakland Harbor entrance lights: the inner red range light was dropped and a new red pile beacon light was erected 240 feet off the end of the south jetty. This is a re-arrangement of the 1890 station, not its establishment. OCR-derived.

Oakland Harbor South Jetty light.quote: Oakland Harbor South Jetty, San Francisco Bay, California.—A lens-lantern light, September 15, 1893.
Oakland Harbor South Jetty light.establishes: The Oakland Harbor South Jetty light was established 15 September 1893. Three days earlier the old rear range light was extinguished — the 1894 report, p. 8, under 'LIGHTS DISCONTINUED': 'Oakland Harbor range (rear), San Francisco Bay, California.—A lens-lantern light, September 12, 1893.' Both OCR-derived.

Oakland Harbor light-house.quote: 889. Oakland Harbor, entrance to Oakland Harbor, California.—The stability of the piles supporting this structure was increased and further oscillation was prevented by filling the space under the building with 2,000 tons of stone. This was quarried on Goat Island and was transported to the station in schooners.
Oakland Harbor light-house.establishes: The pile-founded Oakland Harbor light-house oscillated badly and was stabilized in FY1894 with 2,000 tons of Goat Island (Yerba Buena) stone dumped beneath it. OCR-derived.

San Luis Obispo (Port Harford).quote: 795. San Luis Obispo, near Port Harford, seacoast of California.—The pipe line to convey water from Pecho Creek to the station, commenced in the last fiscal year, was completed in August, and by it an ample supply of good water was obtained. During the winter the heavy rains brought down large quantities of earth and other débris, which clogged the dam and pipes.
San Luis Obispo (Port Harford).establishes: By FY1891 San Luis Obispo was an operating station undergoing water-supply work — i.e. it was established before this report. NULL on the establishment date: no volume I obtained contains the Board's statement of when the San Luis Obispo light was first exhibited. The nearest indirect evidence is the Bodega Head recommendation reprinted in the 1891 report (p. 159) and again in 1893 (p. 166), which describes 'an engine house, such as is being constructed at San Luis Obispo, with duplicate steam fog-signal whistles, and two single dwellings for the keepers, one to have a tower for the light, as at San Luis Obispo' — stale boilerplate first written while the station was still building. Board station number 795 (1891); 15 (1901).

Point Buchon (proposed, never built).station: Point Buchon (proposed, never built) — the Port Harford approach
Point Buchon (proposed, never built).quote: This point is in San Luis Obispo County, and is 17 miles distant from the town of San Luis Obispo by wagon road and trail. The nearest light-house is Piedras Blancas, about 30 nautical miles to the northward and westward. The point is prominent, and with its outlying rocks is very dangerous to navigators close inshore during a fog, especially as vessels going to and from Port Harford make a sharp turn just off this point. It is estimated that a light-house and fog signal can be erected at this point for $33,000.
Point Buchon (proposed, never built).establishes: A standing Board recommendation for a Point Buchon light and fog signal at $33,000, justified by the sharp turn Port Harford traffic makes off the point in fog. WARNING: the OCR of this passage renders the figure as '$83,000'; the page image reads $33,000. Any figure taken from the _djvu.txt of these volumes should be checked against the leaf image.

Point Sur.quote: 797. Point Sur, seacoast of California.—Great trouble was experienced in keeping the rain from driving through the porous stone of which the dwelling walls are built. To prevent this, the Sylvester process, consisting of alternate washes of alum and soap, was tried, but with only partial success.
Point Sur.establishes: Point Sur was an operating station by FY1891, with porous-stone dwelling walls that leaked; the Sylvester process (alternate alum and soap washes) was tried on them. NULL on the establishment date: Point Sur appears in every volume I obtained only under repairs, water supply, road-building and fog-signal running hours — no volume in hand contains the Board's statement of the 1889 first lighting, which belongs to the FY1889 or FY1890 report. Board station number 797 (1891); 859 (1893); 892 (1895); 993 (1896); 17 (1901).

Santa Cruz.quote: 995. Santa Cruz, entrance to Santa Cruz Harbor, California.—This station was connected with the water supply of Santa Cruz City. Various repairs were made.
Santa Cruz.establishes: NULL on Santa Cruz establishment. In all ten obtained report years Santa Cruz appears only in repairs lists, in the whistling-buoy inventory ('Santa Cruz, California.—A second-class whistling buoy, in good condition'), and in this single one-line 1896 note about hooking the station to the city water supply. The Santa Cruz light was established in 1870 and its establishment statement lies in era 1.

Trinidad Head fog bell.quote: 47. Trinidad Head, Pacific Ocean, California.—The fog bell was put in operation July 15, 1898.
Trinidad Head fog bell.establishes: The Trinidad Head fog bell was put in operation 15 July 1898 — a California fog-signal establishment inside this era that the brief did not ask for. Note the Board had earlier refused a bell here: the 1891 report (p. 160, image-verified) records that on 14 November 1890 the district officers reported 'that it was inadvisable to establish such a fog signal there, as the elevation of the station would render the sound of a bell inaudible at sea level.' The same 1899 page adds that $250 was appropriated by the act of 3 March 1899 for a telephone line from the station to Trinidad.

Humboldt Bay jetty lights.station: Humboldt Bay jetty lights — fog signal wanted
Humboldt Bay jetty lights.quote: 41, 42, 43. Humboldt Bay, California.—There are three lights maintained on the jetties to guide vessels in over the bar. These, however, are ineffective in thick or foggy weather by day or night. It is evident that a fog-signal is much needed here. It is estimated that a proper fog-signal can be established on either the north or south jetty at a cost not to exceed $15,000.
Humboldt Bay jetty lights.establishes: Board statement on a California fog-signal deficiency: the three Humboldt Bay jetty lights were useless in fog and the Board asked $15,000 for a jetty fog signal.

Fort Point fog signal and the wreck of t.station: Fort Point fog signal and the wreck of the Rio de Janeiro
Fort Point fog signal and the wreck of t.quote: The present Fort Point fog-signal, a bell struck by machinery, has long been complained of as inadequate, both in position and power. It is proposed to replace it with a second-class Daboll trumpet, blown by compressed air, and to place it on the top of the northwest bastion of Fort Winfield Scott, Fort Point, California, which will bring it directly over the present location of the bell. It is estimated that this can be done for not exceeding $7,000, and it is recommended that an appropriation of this amount be made therefor. The importance of this aid to navigation can not be urged too strongly. The bell can be heard only over a very limited area, frequently not at all until abreast of the fort. An efficient signal should be heard considerably to seaward to give warning of the approach to the vicinity of Fort Point Shoal. The recent disaster to the steamer Rio de Janeiro on this reef, involving a loss of over 100 lives, might not have occurred if an efficient signal had been in operation here.
Fort Point fog signal and the wreck of t.establishes: The sharpest Board statement on the failure of California bell fog signals in this era: the Fort Point bell was inadequate 'both in position and power', audible only abreast of the fort, and the Board explicitly connects the loss of the steamer City of Rio de Janeiro on Fort Point Shoal (over 100 lives, February 1901) to that inadequacy. A second-class compressed-air Daboll trumpet on the northwest bastion of Fort Winfield Scott was proposed at $7,000. The Board also decided to fit a new fourth-order lens at Fort Point.

Southampton Shoal (proposed) and Karquin.quote: The Board is of opinion that the interests of commerce and navigation demand the establishment of a fog bell and lens-lantern light on the southeast end of this shoal. It is proposed to build a frame dwelling for the keeper on iron piles, with gallery and bell house, the signal to be a 3,000-pound bell struck by a Stevens apparatus, the lens lantern to be exhibited from the corner of the gallery. It is estimated that the entire structure can be built for a sum not exceeding $30,000, and the Board recommends that an appropriation of this amount be made therefor.
Southampton Shoal (proposed) and Karquin.establishes: Board proposal for Southampton Shoal light and fog bell at $30,000, justified by the new Santa Fe Railroad ferry from San Francisco to Point Richmond established during FY1901, whose straight course runs close to the shoal's southeast point. On the same page the Board asks $50,000 for a light and fog signal in Karquines Strait opposite the Selby Smelting Works.

Alcatraz fog-signal station (new, north.quote: 29. Alcatraz Fog-Signal Station, San Francisco Bay, California.—This new fog-signal station, established on the northern end of the island, consists of a small frame structure for housing the clockwork striking apparatus, with a 3,000-pound fog bell mounted in front.
Alcatraz fog-signal station (new, north.establishes: A new fog-signal station was established at the north end of Alcatraz Island in FY1901, with a 3,000-pound bell and clockwork striking apparatus. Foreshadowed by the 1900 report (p. 179, OCR only): '27. Alcatraz Island, San Francisco Bay, California.—The fog bell was moved from its original site to a position on higher ground 140 feet to the northward and set up, with a new striking apparatus, in a new building.'

Point Arguello.page: p. 11 (NEW LIGHTS) and pp. 200–201 (fog signal); p. 11 image-verified
Point Arguello.quote: Point Arguello light-station, seacoast of California.—A fourth-order light February 22, 1901.
Point Arguello.establishes: Point Arguello light first exhibited 22 February 1901, fourth order; its compressed-air siren was established 1 June 1901 — the 1901 report (p. 201, OCR only) records: '14. Point Arguello, California.—This first-class siren, in duplicate, operated by 13-horsepower oil engines and compressed air, was in operation about 84 hours since the date of its establishment, June 1, 1901, and consumed some 171 gallons of oil.' This was the fog signal the Board then held up as the model for Quarry Point. The station had been recommended since at least the FY1889 report at an estimated $35,000 (1891 report, p. 157, image-verified: 'It is reported to be one of the foggiest places on the Pacific coast').

Point Arguello.report_year: FY1900 (Annual Report of the Light-House Board for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1900; Twelfth District)
Point Arguello.quote: 12. Point Arguello, about 12 miles northwest of Point Conception, seacoast of California.—The act approved March 3, 1899, appropriated $35,000 for establishing a light-house and fog-signal on this point. Since the passage of the act much time has been consumed in obtaining the right to take water from a spring on land adjoining the reservation and in securing rights of way to the county road. These matters being satisfactorily adjusted, bids for the construction of the station were opened on March 22, 1900, and the contract was let for $17,000. Actual construction work will probably be commenced early in July, 1900.
Point Arguello.establishes: Authorization and funding for Point Arguello: act of 3 March 1899, $35,000; construction contract let 22 March 1900 for $17,000; work to begin early July 1900 — i.e. exactly the timetable that produced a station lit in 1901. CAVEAT: this is the FY1900 report, not the FY1901 report. The FY1901 volume, which would carry the Board's own statement of the date of first lighting, could not be obtained (see gaps).

Point Arguello.report_year: FY1905 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor: 1905; Report of the Light-House Board, 'Fog-signals operated by steam or oil engines')
Point Arguello.quote: 16. Point Arguello, California.—This 12-inch whistle, in duplicate, worked by a 13-horsepower oil engine and compressed air, was in operation some 540 hours and consumed about 1,150 gallons of mineral oil.
Point Arguello.establishes: Point Arguello was a fully operating light and fog-signal station by FY1905 — a 12-inch whistle in duplicate driven by a 13-hp oil engine, run 540 hours in the year. This is the earliest in-service statement I could obtain for the station; it confirms establishment before 30 June 1905 but does not give the 1901 date.

Point Arguello.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Point Arguello.quote: 15. Point Arguello, about 12 miles northwest of Point Conception, seacoast of California.—The construction of a 40,000-gallon concrete cistern was completed. The cistern is 24 feet internal diameter, with wall 1 foot thick. ... A rectangular sheet-steel oil tank of 1,800 gallons capacity was installed for supplying the oil engines operating the air-compressor plant for a fog-signal.
Point Arguello.establishes: Continued station improvements at Point Arguello in FY1907 (40,000-gallon concrete cistern; 1,800-gallon oil tank for the fog-signal air compressors), confirming a manned station dependent on trucked/piped water in this exposed location.

Twelfth District fog signals generally.station: Twelfth District fog signals generally — the 1891 fog season
Twelfth District fog signals generally.quote: The length of time fog prevailed throughout this entire district from August to December, 1891, is without precedent. The season was unusually mild, with little or none of the strong trade winds, which usually blow every day from noon till sunset, during the summer months. Hence the fogs hung along the coast line with a peculiar tenacity. Every fog signal in the district, except that at Point Arena, was in operation a greater number of hours than during the previous year. This resulted in an increased expenditure of fuel and a consequent increase in the expenses of the tender for transportation. The signals were in operation last year some 13,520 hours on a consumption of about 596 tons of coal and 508 cords of wood, while during the previous year they were in operation some 9,958 hours, with an expenditure of about 434 tons of coal and 436 cords of wood.
Twelfth District fog signals generally.establishes: The Board's own account of an anomalous California fog season, August–December 1891, attributed to the failure of the summer trade winds: 13,520 aggregate fog-signal hours in the Twelfth District against 9,958 the previous year, 596 tons of coal and 508 cords of wood against 434 and 436. Every district signal except Point Arena ran longer than the year before.

Twelfth District.station: Twelfth District — scale of the establishment
Twelfth District.quote: This district extends from the boundary line between California and Mexico to the boundary line between California and Oregon, a distance of about 800 miles of coast line, and embraces all the aids to navigation on the seacoast, bays, and navigable rivers of California. Inspector.—Lieut. Commander Thomas Perry, U. S. Navy. Engineer.—Maj. William H. Heuer, Corps of Engineers, U. S. Army.
Twelfth District.establishes: Baseline inventory for California as of 30 June 1891: 36 light-houses and lighted beacons; 1 light-ship in position; 48 day or unlighted beacons; 14 fog signals operated by steam; 7 fog signals operated by clockwork; 12 whistling buoys; 5 bell buoys; 83 other buoys; the tender Madroño and the steam launch Hazel. District officers named: Lieut. Cdr. Thomas Perry (Inspector) and Maj. William H. Heuer (Engineer).

Bodega Head (proposed, never built).quote: Fog, accompanied by northwest winds, varying from fresh to strong in force, prevails above Point Reyes during about nine months of the year. The currents are uncertain in direction either up or down the coast, and seem to be due to causes which exist far to the north. ... A fog signal at this locality would therefore be of great benefit to mariners, and a small light would also be of much service, at little additional expense, as there is a stretch of unlighted territory about 68 miles in length between Point Reyes and Point Arena.
Bodega Head (proposed, never built).establishes: Board reasoning for a Bodega Head light and fog signal at $30,000: fog nine months a year above Point Reyes, unreliable currents, and a 68-mile unlighted gap between Point Reyes and Point Arena. Recommendation renewed from at least the FY1889 report; the station was never built.

Carquinez Strait.report_year: FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; 'Report of the Operations of the Light-House Board')
Carquinez Strait.quote: Carquinez Strait light-station, California.—The act approved March 4, 1907, appropriated $50,000 for the establishment of a light and fog-signal station at Carquinez Strait, between San Pablo Bay and Suisun Bay, authorized by the act approved February 26, 1907. The actual work of construction was commenced August 4, 1908. The station was established January 15, 1910. A fourth-order fixed red light and two gasoline-engine compressed-air plants operating 6-inch first-class compressed-air sirens were installed. The superstructure consists of a frame tower for the light, a frame dwelling with quarters for three keepers, a frame fog-signal house, a frame boathouse, a galvanized-iron oil house, and distillate house. A water pipe connects with the Vallejo city mains. Total cost of constructing station, $48,296.17.
Carquinez Strait.establishes: THE ESTABLISHMENT STATEMENT. Carquinez Strait Light Station was established 15 January 1910. Authorized by act of 26 Feb. 1907; $50,000 appropriated by act of 4 March 1907; construction begun 4 Aug. 1908; fourth-order fixed red light plus two 6-inch first-class compressed-air sirens; quarters for three keepers; total cost $48,296.17; water piped from the Vallejo city mains.

Carquinez Strait.report_year: FY1909 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1909; Light-House Board, 'Uncompleted works of construction')
Carquinez Strait.quote: Carquinez Strait, California.—Authorized by the act of February 26, 1907, at a cost not to exceed $50,000; appropriation, act of March 4, 1907, $50,000. During the year the contractor commenced work on the landing and approach, the station substructure on piles, and on the superstructure, the latter consisting of a light and fog-signal building, boathouse, and three sets of keepers' quarters. At the close of the year he had practically completed the station substructure and the landing and approach. The superstructure is about 65 per cent completed. As soon as the contract is completed, which will probably be in July of the coming year, the fourth-order lens, lantern, fog-signal machinery, and 6-inch standard sirens, which are all on hand, will be installed, and the station should be ready for operation about October 1, 1909.
Carquinez Strait.establishes: Construction progress as of 30 June 1909, and the Board's own (over-optimistic) forecast that the station 'should be ready for operation about October 1, 1909' — three and a half months before the actual 15 January 1910 establishment. Confirms the pile substructure and three sets of keepers' quarters.

Carquinez Strait.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Carquinez Strait.quote: 44. Carquinez Strait, between San Pablo and Suisun Bay, California.—The act approved on March 4, 1907, appropriated $50,000 for establishing a light and fog-signal at Carquinez Strait station. Plans were made and the work will be commenced soon.
Carquinez Strait.establishes: The earliest stage: the $50,000 appropriation of 4 March 1907 and the making of plans. Note that in this same district list the Board still carries 'Mare Island' as station no. 42 and Carquinez Strait as station no. 44 — i.e. the two stations coexisted in the Board's numbering before Mare Island was discontinued.

Mare Island.report_year: FY1918 (Reports of the Department of Commerce, 1918; Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses)
Mare Island.quote: The act of July 1, 1918, making appropriations for the naval service for the fiscal year 1919, transferred to the Navy Department the unused Mare Island Light Station, Cal. This station was discontinued July 1, 1917, and is not further required for lighthouse purposes.
Mare Island.establishes: THE DISCONTINUANCE STATEMENT, in the agency's own words: Mare Island Light Station was discontinued 1 July 1917 and was 'not further required for lighthouse purposes'; the site and structures were transferred to the Navy Department by the naval appropriation act of 1 July 1918. The volume's index confirms the entry: 'Mare Island, Cal., light station discontinued.. 567' and 'Mare Island Light Station, Cal., transferred. 567'.

Mare Island.report_year: FY1917 (Reports of the Department of Commerce, 1917; Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, table 'Lights discontinued during the fiscal year 1917')
Mare Island.quote: LIGHTS DISCONTINUED DURING THE FISCAL YEAR 1917. [158 lights, including float lights.] ... 18th ... Mare Island, Cal.
Mare Island.establishes: Mare Island appears as a table row among lights discontinued in FY1917 (18th lighthouse district). CAUTION: this is a table entry, not a sentence, and the OCR of the district column in this table is badly garbled, so the district assignment is my reading rather than a clean transcription. It also sits one day on the other side of the line from the FY1918 narrative, which dates the discontinuance to 1 July 1917 (the first day of FY1918). Treat the FY1918 p. 567 sentence as the authoritative agency statement and this table as corroboration only.

Mare Island.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Mare Island.quote: 42. Mare Island, entrance to Carquinez Strait, San Pablo Bay, California.—Repairs to the lens at this station were made. A fog-bell striking apparatus was installed, replacing an old one.
Mare Island.establishes: Mare Island was a going concern with a lens and a bell fog signal in FY1907, and the Board located it 'at the entrance to Carquinez Strait' — the agency's own geographic framing of the station that Carquinez Strait would supersede.

Point Cabrillo.report_year: FY1909 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1909; Light-House Board, 'Works of construction completed')
Point Cabrillo.quote: Point Cabrillo, California.—This station, on Point Cabrillo, consisting of a light and fog-signal building, three keeper's dwellings, barn, pump house, water-supply system, carpenter and blacksmith shops, was completed on June 10, 1909, at a cost of $50,000. The light is of the third order, flashing white every 10 seconds, 84 feet above the water, and should be visible 14 1/2 miles in clear weather. The fog signal is a 6-inch compressed-air siren.
Point Cabrillo.establishes: THE COMPLETION STATEMENT. Point Cabrillo Light Station completed 10 June 1909 at a cost of $50,000; third-order lens flashing white every 10 seconds; focal plane 84 feet above the water; visible 14.5 miles; 6-inch compressed-air siren; three keepers' dwellings.

Point Cabrillo.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Point Cabrillo.quote: 68. Point Cabrillo, about 4 miles north of Mendocino city, seacoast of California.—The act approved on June 30, 1906, authorized a contract for the construction of a light and fog-signal, at a cost not to exceed $50,000, and appropriated $25,000 therefor. The site for the light-station was selected, surveyed, and measures are being taken to obtain title to this site.
Point Cabrillo.establishes: Authorization and funding: act of 30 June 1906 authorized the contract at a limit of $50,000 and appropriated $25,000; site selected and surveyed in FY1907. Also fixes the Board's own locational description, 'about 4 miles north of Mendocino city.'

Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (printe.station: Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (printed as San Pedro Breakwater Light Station)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (printe.report_year: FY1913 (Reports of the Department of Commerce, 1913; Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, descriptive section)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (printe.quote: SAN PEDRO BREAKWATER LIGHT STATION, CAL. Purpose.—San Pedro Breakwater Light and Fog Signal Station was established to mark the outer end of the breakwater and to guide vessels into Los Angeles Harbor, Cal. This station went into commission March 1, 1913.
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (printe.establishes: THE ESTABLISHMENT STATEMENT plus the agency's explicit statement of WHY the station was built. The light now known as Los Angeles Harbor Light / Angels Gate went into commission 1 March 1913; its stated purpose was to mark the outer end of the San Pedro breakwater and guide vessels into Los Angeles Harbor. Note the Bureau's own name for it in 1913 was 'San Pedro Breakwater Light Station'.

Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.station: Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pedro Breakwater)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.report_year: FY1913 (Reports of the Department of Commerce, 1913; Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, construction narrative)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.quote: San Pedro Breakwater, Cal.—The act of March 4, 1911, appropriated $36,000 for establishing a light and fog signal station on the San Pedro Breakwater, Cal. The lighthouse was completed during the year and placed in commission on March 1, 1913. It consists of a structural steel framework, the lower section containing fog-signal machinery, being built of metal plate. The upper section is built of cement plaster on metal lath and contains quarters for three keepers. The light apparatus is a fourth-order flashing bivalve lens with oil vapor lamp, of approximately 69,000 candlepower, shown at a height of 73 feet above the water. The fog signal is a first-class compressed-air siren; compressor and gas engine are direct connected, and the plant is in duplicate. The total cost to June 30, 1913, was $35,225.58.
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.establishes: Appropriation ($36,000, act of 4 March 1911), date of first lighting/commissioning (1 March 1913), order of lens (fourth-order flashing bivalve, ~69,000 candlepower, focal plane 73 feet), fog signal (first-class compressed-air siren in duplicate), and cost to 30 June 1913 ($35,225.58). The descriptive section at p. 414 gives the final figure: 'the total cost was $35,971.49 ... the station was completed in June, 1913.'

Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.station: Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pedro Breakwater)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.report_year: FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; Light-House Board recommendations, Group No. 2)
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.quote: No. 7. San Pedro Breakwater light-station, Cal.—For establishing a light and fog-signal station on the San Pedro Breakwater, Cal., $36,000. San Pedro Breakwater has been completed and the harbor developed. It should be marked by a light and fog-signal. Numerous petitions have been received from maritime interests urging the same.
Los Angeles Harbor / Angels Gate (San Pe.establishes: The Light-House Board's own stated reason for the station, three years before it was lit: the breakwater was complete, the harbor developed, and maritime interests had petitioned. Also fixes the $36,000 estimate that Congress appropriated in the act of 4 March 1911.

Point Stuart (Angel Island).report_year: FY1915 (Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses ... for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1915)
Point Stuart (Angel Island).quote: Fog signals established: Gallups Island, Boston Harbor, Mass. (electric bell); Fort McHenry, Baltimore Harbor, Md. (electric bell); Volusia Bar, St. Johns River, Fla. (bell); Point Blunt and Point Stuart, Angel Island, San Francisco Bay, Cal. (electric sirens).
Point Stuart (Angel Island).establishes: Point Stuart (with Point Blunt) on Angel Island received an ELECTRIC SIREN fog signal established during the fiscal year ended 30 June 1915. Note precisely what this sentence does and does not say: it is the Bureau's list of FOG SIGNALS established, not of lights. The same volume's table of 'Works under special appropriations, completed during fiscal year 1915' carries the corresponding entry 'Angel Island, Cal. (Point Blunt Light; Point Stuart Light) ... Installation of electric lights and electric fog signals controlled from Angel Island Station; also enlarging keepers quarters at Angel Island Station,' which is the Bureau's own statement that the Point Stuart light and fog signal were installed as remote-controlled electric aids worked from the Angel Island station. I could not find a page number in the OCR for that table.

Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.report_year: FY1905 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor: 1905; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.quote: 58. Blunts Reef light-vessel, No. 83, off Cape Mendocino, California.—This steel steam self-propelling light-vessel, of about 621 tons displacement, for which appropriation was made by the act approved on March 3, 1903, arrived in San Francisco in company with relief light-vessel No. 76 on June 4, 1905, at 1 a. m., after a successful voyage of 110 days from New York, of which time she was under steam 82 1/2 days. This vessel was docked, when her bottom was painted. After receiving coal, fresh water, and supplies she was again fitted for sea, and on June 28 took station off Blunts Reef in accordance with the published notice to mariners.
Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.establishes: THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE BLUNTS REEF LIGHTSHIP STATION: Light-Vessel No. 83 'took station off Blunts Reef' on 28 JUNE 1905, two days before the close of the fiscal year. Appropriation by act of 3 March 1903; 621 tons displacement; arrived San Francisco 4 June 1905 after a 110-day voyage from New York.

Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.report_year: FY1904 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1904; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.quote: 58. Blunts Reef light-vessel, No. 83, off Cape Mendocino, seacoast of California.—The act approved on March 3, 1903, appropriated $90,000 for constructing, equipping, and outfitting, complete for service, a first-class steam light-vessel, with steam fog-signal, to be situated off this cape. ... She is now being built by contract, under which she is to be delivered by December 17, 1904. She will be sent to the Pacific coast as soon as practicable after she is finished.
Blunts Reef lightship station (Light-Ves.establishes: The appropriation ($90,000, act of 3 March 1903) and the Board's purpose — 'a first-class steam light-vessel, with steam fog-signal, to be situated off this cape' [Cape Mendocino] — plus the contract delivery date of 17 Dec. 1904. The FY1907 report (p. 601 region) adds that she 'was built at Camden, N. J., in 1904.'

Anacapa Island.report_year: FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; Light-House Board recommendations, Group No. 3)
Anacapa Island.quote: No. 2. Anacapa Island light-station, Cal.—For the establishment of a light and fog-signal station on Anacapa Island, Cal., $100,000. Anacapa Island is one of the most difficult points on the southern California coast to pass in bad weather, and it is important that a light and fog-signal be established. The act of June 17, 1910, authorized this station, but no appropriation has been made therefor.
Anacapa Island.establishes: THE AGENCY'S STATEMENT OF WHY Anacapa was to be lit, and the authorizing act: the act of 17 June 1910 authorized an Anacapa light and fog-signal station at a limit of $100,000, but Congress voted no money. This explains why only a small unattended beacon appeared in 1912 rather than a full station.

Anacapa Island.report_year: FY1914 (Reports of the Department of Commerce, 1914; Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, estimates)
Anacapa Island.quote: No. 56. Anacapa Island, Cal., Light Station.—For establishing a light and fog signal at or near Anacapa Island, Cal., $103,000. NOTE.—Practically all coastwise vessels and a large number of those bound for Panama use the Santa Barbara Channel, and this traffic will be greatly increased with the opening of the Panama Canal. The desirable course leads close to the eastern end of Anacapa Island, which is now marked by a small beacon light, not sufficiently powerful to be of service in hazy weather. The American Shipmaster's Association has presented a petition for a light and fog signal, indorsed by the San Francisco and Los Angeles chambers of commerce and important shipping interests on the Pacific coast. It is therefore recommended that a light of high candle power and a first-class fog signal be established at this point as soon as practicable.
Anacapa Island.establishes: The Bureau's own confirmation that by FY1914 Anacapa's eastern end WAS ALREADY MARKED by 'a small beacon light' — corroborating that a minor unattended light existed there by 1912-14 — together with the reasons for wanting a full station (Panama Canal traffic through the Santa Barbara Channel; petitions from the American Shipmasters' Association and the San Francisco and Los Angeles chambers of commerce). The $103,000 estimate breaks down as light tower $9,000(?), illuminating apparatus $8,500, fog-signal building and apparatus $14,000, etc.

Anacapa Island.report_year: FY1907 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1907; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Anacapa Island.quote: Santa Barbara channel islands, California.—Three islands of this group, San Clemente, Anacapa, and San Nicolas, are reserved for light-house purposes. San Clemente was leased for a period of five years from January 1, 1906, at $1,000 per annum. Anacapa was leased to the highest bidder for five years from April 1, 1907, at $31 a year. San Nicolas was leased to the highest bidder for five years commencing on April 15, 1907, at $362.60 a year.
Anacapa Island.establishes: Anacapa Island was a light-house reservation from well before it was lit, and the Board leased it out (for $31 a year from 1 April 1907) while it waited for money to build. Useful for the land-tenure history of the station.

Southampton Shoal.report_year: FY1904 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1904; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Southampton Shoal.quote: 46. Southampton Shoal, San Francisco Bay, California.—The act approved on March 3, 1903, appropriated $30,000 for establishing a light and fog-signal to mark the south end of the shoal. Plans and specifications were prepared.
Southampton Shoal.establishes: The authorizing appropriation ($30,000, act of 3 March 1903) and the agency's statement of PURPOSE — 'to mark the south end of the shoal.' The Board's adjacent discussion (pp. 279-280) explains the hazard: the passage between the east side of Angel Island and Southampton Shoal 'is quite narrow,' strong Golden Gate tides set vessels onto it, and the ship Mauladen 'while being towed to Port Costa, ran ashore on Southampton Shoal.'

Southampton Shoal.report_year: FY1905 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor: 1905; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Southampton Shoal.quote: 46. Southampton Shoal, San Francisco Bay, California.—The act approved on March 3, 1903, appropriated $30,000 for a light and fog-signal to mark the southern end of this shoal. A contract was made in March, 1905, to build a light-house consisting of a substructure of iron cylinders filled with concrete, carrying a platform of steel beams and concrete arches upon which will rest the frame dwelling, surmounted by a light tower. The eleven supporting cylinders are in place and the steel frame of the platform is in position.
Southampton Shoal.establishes: Construction state at 30 June 1905: contract let March 1905; eleven concrete-filled iron cylinders in place; steel platform frame set; the frame dwelling surmounted by a light tower still to come. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE FINDING: the station was NOT yet in operation at the close of FY1905, so the actual first lighting falls in FY1906 — the one volume I could not obtain.

Southampton Shoal.report_year: FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; Light-House Board recommendations, Group No. 3)
Southampton Shoal.quote: No. 1. Fort Point fog-signal, Cal.—For the substitution of a first-class fog-signal to replace the present Daboll trumpet at the Fort Point light-station, Cal., $11,000. The present fog-signal at Fort Point, which is inadequate for this important station, is to be installed to replace the present bell fog-signal at Southampton Shoal light-station.
Southampton Shoal.establishes: Southampton Shoal Light Station was in operation with a BELL fog signal by FY1910, and the Board planned to hand it Fort Point's cast-off Daboll trumpet. This is the earliest statement in the volumes I obtained that shows the station as a working light-station rather than a construction project.

Mile Rocks.report_year: FY1905 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor: 1905; Report of the Light-House Board, Twelfth District)
Mile Rocks.quote: 28. Mile Rocks, southern side of channel, entrance to San Francisco Bay, California.—Contracts were made for building the concrete and steel substructure and also for the steel superstructure of the station. Work under the first contract was commenced in August, 1904, when a working party landed on the rock and commenced preparing it, by cutting and blasting, to receive the foundations of the building. In September, 1904, a schooner fitted as quarters for the workmen and for the storage of materials was moored close to the rock, but during a heavy blow she dragged her moorings and barely escaped being wrecked. ... The work was difficult and hazardous during its early stages, and proceeded slowly on account of the exposed position of Mile Rocks, directly in the entrance to San Francisco Harbor, where it is subjected to all the violence of the sea. There was hardly a day during the year on which at some time the waves did not break over the rock. There were many days when no landing could be effected and many others when the party, after landing, was driven off with only a few hours of work accomplished. On several occasions it was necessary to call upon the neighboring life-saving crews to take the men off the rock. A full day of eight hours passed upon the rock was exceptional until after the substructure was completed in June, 1905. This consists of a monolith of concrete inclosed within steel plates resting on the rock at the level of mean high water. It is elliptical in plan, covering 704 square feet, and has a height of 34 feet; 1,006 barrels of cement, furnished by the Government, were used in the work.
Mile Rocks.establishes: The Board's own detailed account of building Mile Rocks: work begun August 1904, substructure completed JUNE 1905 (elliptical concrete monolith in steel plating, 704 sq. ft., 34 ft high, 1,006 barrels of cement). It also gives the agency's framing of the site's danger. The station was still incomplete at the close of FY1905; the lighting (February 1906) falls in the FY1906 report, which I could not obtain.

Mile Rocks.quote: 27. Mile Rocks, entrance to Golden Gate, San Francisco Bay, California.—Two derricks for receiving supplies on the east and west sides of the station were installed.
